summary: After hearing that Lazarus is ill, Jesus delays before traveling to Bethany. Martha confesses him as Messiah and Son of God; Mary and the mourners bring him to the tomb, where Jesus weeps, commands the stone removed, prays, and calls Lazarus out. The sign produces belief and alarm, and Caiaphas unknowingly prophesies that Jesus will die for the nation and gather God's scattered children.
whyItMatters: John places the Gospel's most public life-giving sign in the shadow of Jesus's own death. Jesus is neither detached from grief nor trapped by it: he loves, weeps, is deeply moved, and acts. Resurrection is not only a last-day doctrine but a person encountered now, while Lazarus's restored mortal life points beyond itself to Jesus's coming victory.

context.author: The Gospel's unnamed writer, whose testimony the book ties to the beloved disciple and early tradition to John son of Zebedee (authorship is debated), bringing the sign sequence to a climax that directly triggers the death plot
context.audience: Readers at some distance from the Judean world, for whom John explains where Bethany lay (11:18); the chapter involves mourning, tombs, resurrection hope, and high-priestly politics under Rome
context.date: Commonly dated around AD 90–100, with some proposing earlier stages or a broader late-first-century range; the story occurs shortly before the final Passover, with Bethany near Jerusalem
context.setting: Where Jesus was staying (beyond the Jordan, 10:40), then Bethany at the family home and the cave tomb, followed by a council of chief priests and Pharisees
context.literaryForm: Delay-and-journey narrative, two encounter scenes, climactic sign, and political aftermath shaped by dramatic irony

outline.heading: News, love, delay, and the dangerous return to Judea
outline.note: The sisters send word that Lazarus is sick; Jesus stays two days, then tells the disciples plainly 'Lazarus is dead'

outline.heading: Martha meets the resurrection and the life
outline.note: Martha meets Jesus, who says 'I am the resurrection and the life'; she answers that she believes he is the Christ

outline.heading: Mary, mourners, and Jesus approach the tomb in grief
outline.note: Martha calls Mary secretly; Mary falls at Jesus's feet, and troubled Jesus asks 'Where have you laid him'; then 'Jesus wept'

outline.heading: Jesus calls Lazarus from the tomb
outline.note: Jesus has the stone taken away from the cave, thanks the Father, and cries 'Lazarus, come out'; the dead man comes out bound

outline.heading: Belief and fear lead the council to plan Jesus's death
outline.note: The council fears the Romans will take away their place and nation; Caiaphas says one man should die for the people

keyVerses.text: Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies.
keyVerses.why: Jesus locates resurrection hope in relation to himself, present even before the last day.

keyVerses.text: They told him, “Lord, come and see.” Jesus wept.
keyVerses.why: The giver of life fully enters human grief rather than treating mourning as ignorance.

keyVerses.text: When he had said this, he cried with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!”
keyVerses.why: Jesus's commanding voice enacts the life-giving authority announced in chapter 5.

questions.question: Why does Jesus delay if he loves the family?
questions.answer: John emphatically joins the facts: Jesus loves Martha, Mary, and Lazarus; therefore, after hearing, he remains two days. The delay is not indifference or proof that grief is unreal. It lets Lazarus's death become unmistakable and the sign reveal God's glory, while the rest of the story shows the cost borne by the family and by Jesus himself.

questions.question: Why call death ‘sleep’?
questions.answer: Sleep is a biblical metaphor for death (Daniel 12:2) that can suggest death's temporary character before awakening. The disciples hear it literally and think Lazarus will recover, so Jesus speaks plainly: Lazarus died. John uses misunderstanding to disclose hope, not to deny death or say that bereaved people should speak euphemistically.

questions.question: What makes Martha's confession so important?
questions.answer: Martha already trusts that God hears Jesus and affirms resurrection ‘at the last day,’ a hope present in some Jewish traditions (Daniel 12:2). Jesus does not discard that future hope; he centers it in himself. She then confesses him as Messiah, Son of God, and the one coming into the world—one of John's fullest confessions before the cross.

questions.question: How can Jesus weep when he knows he will raise Lazarus?
questions.answer: Knowledge of the outcome does not cancel love's encounter with present loss. The verb dakryō in verse 35 depicts tears; Jesus also sees Mary and the community weeping. John holds divine authority and genuine human grief together. Christian hope should likewise make room for lament rather than treating tears as failed faith.

questions.question: What does ‘groaned in the spirit’ mean?
questions.answer: The Greek embrimaomai can convey strong agitation, indignation, or a snorting intensity, stronger than quiet sadness. Interpreters differ over whether Jesus is angry at death, unbelief, the mourning scene, or some combination. Together with ‘troubled,’ the word presents him confronting the tomb with emotional force, not serene detachment.

questions.question: Why pray publicly before calling Lazarus?
questions.answer: Jesus thanks the Father for already hearing him and explicitly says the public prayer is for the crowd, so they may believe the Father sent him. The sign is not a magician's independent display. It reveals the shared work of Father and Son and makes Jesus's mission the issue the witnesses must decide.

questions.question: Why must others remove the stone and unbind Lazarus?
questions.answer: Jesus alone calls the dead man to life, yet he commands the community to remove the stone and release the grave cloths. The details make the physical restoration concrete and invite participation around an act only Jesus can accomplish. Lazarus returns to ordinary mortal life (12:10 shows he can still be killed); he emerges still wrapped, which many readers contrast with the cloths left in Jesus's tomb (20:7).

questions.question: How can Caiaphas prophesy while plotting Jesus's death?
questions.answer: As high priest he argues the brutal logic of imperial survival: sacrifice one person so the Romans will not ‘take away both our place and our nation.’ The narrator hears more than Caiaphas intends. Jesus will indeed die ‘for the nation,’ but also to gather God's scattered children into one. Dramatic irony turns political expediency into an unwitting statement of Jesus's saving death without excusing the plot.

glossary.def: A village near Jerusalem associated with Martha, Mary, and Lazarus.
To be deeply agitated or indignant; a forceful term for Jesus's response near the tomb.
High priest in the period, whose political counsel John presents as unintended prophecy.
